# 7.1-7.16 TRACE/OUTPUT DRILLS

Each drill gives you real-shaped output. For each, state what happened and what it implies. Do these with the terminal open; half the value is in reproducing them.

## Drill 1: A `curl -v` transcript with a reused connection

```
$ curl -v --http2 https://api.example.com/v1/orders -o /dev/null
*   Trying 203.0.113.10:443...
* Connected to api.example.com (203.0.113.10) port 443 (#0)
* ALPN: server accepted h2
* TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, Certificate (IN):
* TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, CertificateVerify (IN):
* TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, Finished (IN):
* TLSv1.3 (OUT), TLS handshake, ClientHello (OUT):
* TLSv1.3 (OUT), TLS handshake, Finished (OUT):
* using HTTP/2
> GET /v1/orders HTTP/2
> host: api.example.com
> accept: */*
>
< HTTP/2 200
< content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
< cache-control: private, no-store
< x-request-id: 01JB2Q7W3K9F
< content-length: 18422
<
$ curl -v --http2 https://api.example.com/v1/orders -o /dev/null
*   Trying 203.0.113.10:443...
* Connected to api.example.com (203.0.113.10) port 443 (#0)
* ALPN: server accepted h2
* using HTTP/2
* Request completely sent off
> GET /v1/orders HTTP/2
> host: api.example.com
> accept: */*
>
< HTTP/2 200
< x-request-id: 01JB2Q7WA2M4
<
* Connection #0 to host api.example.com left intact
```

**What happened:** the second invocation skipped the entire TLS handshake block. curl uses a **connection pool** in the same process, so the second request reused the open socket.
**What it implies:** the handshake cost in your measurements is paid once per process, not once per request. A benchmark that runs one `curl` per request overstates TLS cost massively. `Connection #0 ... left intact` confirms HTTP/2 keep-alive, so stream 3 (or whichever) opened on the existing connection. The absence of `content-type` and `content-length` in the second response's printed headers is just curl's header echo being deduplicated for identical values, not missing headers.

## Drill 2: `curl -w` timing breakdown

```
$ curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'dns=%{time_namelookup} tcp=%{time_connect} tls=%{time_appconnect} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total} http=%{http_version} size=%{size_download} speed=%{speed_download}\n' https://api.example.com/v1/orders
dns=0.0312 tcp=0.0891 tls=0.1403 ttfb=0.8120 total=0.8841 http=2 size=18422 speed=198000
```

**Read it:**
- DNS: 31 ms — a real lookup, so nothing cached; 0.0000 would mean cached.
- TCP: 89 ms total since start, so **pure TCP = 89 − 31 = 58 ms** ⇒ a ~58 ms RTT path.
- TLS: 140 − 89 = **51 ms** of TLS, slightly less than a full RTT ⇒ **0-RTT resumption** succeeded (the TLS 1.3 handshake was absorbed into the flight).
- TTFB: 812 − 140 = **672 ms of server think time**. This is the number to attack.
- Total: 884 − 812 = 72 ms to move 18 KB ⇒ ~200 KB/s effective, which is slow; check whether compression was negotiated.
- **Implication:** 76% of the request is server time. The transport is a rounding error. And with a 58 ms RTT, a 3-RTT cold path is 174 ms before the server starts working — which is why connection reuse matters so much on this link.

## Drill 3: `dig` with a negative answer

```
$ dig +noall +answer +comments api-v2.example.com A
;; Query time: 8 msec
;; SERVER: 10.0.0.53#53(10.0.0.53)  (UDP)
;; WHEN: Thu Oct 01 09:14:02 UTC 2026

;; AUTHORITY SECTION:
example.com.		3600	IN	SOA	ns1.example.com. hostmaster.example.com. 2026100101 7200 3600 1209600 300
```

**What happened:** the status is NOERROR with **no answer record** (the AUTHORITY section shows the SOA used to derive the negative TTL).
**What it implies:** the name exists in the zone, but has no `A` record. This is **not** NXDOMAIN and **not** an outage — it's a partially-published deploy. The negative cache TTL is `min(SOA.MINIMUM=300, SOA.TTL=3600)` = **300 s**, so this hard failure will persist for up to 5 minutes even after you add the record. **Fix:** publish the record, then wait out the negative TTL, or bump the serial and verify with `dig @1.1.1.1` (a resolver with a clean cache) before declaring success.

## Drill 4: `dig` with truncation

```
$ dig +noall +comments +answer +authority example.com MX
;; Truncated, retrying in TCP mode.
;; communications error to 127.0.0.1#53: connection refused - ignored
;; QUESTION SECTION:
;example.com.			IN	MX
;; AUTHORITY SECTION:
example.com.		900	IN	SOA	ns1.example.com. hostmaster.example.com. 1 7200 3600 1209600 900
```

**What happened:** the response came back at 512 bytes with the TC (truncated) bit set, so dig automatically retried over TCP — and that retry failed because nothing is listening on 127.0.0.1:53.
**What it implies:** DNS over UDP is capped at 512 bytes unless EDNS0 negotiates a larger buffer. If TCP is unavailable (this happens with a broken local resolver, or a resolver with a firewall blocking large TCP/53 responses), you lose the records. **Check for an EDNS0 issue** (`dig +edns=0` to see the advertised UDP size) and for large MX/TXT/DNSSEC responses. Also note the authority section is empty, which means this is a **negative** answer for MX specifically — the domain has no MX record.

## Drill 5: DevTools waterfall reading

```
Name              Protocol  Status  DNS  Initial  SSL  Req  Waiting  Content
                  Type              conn.  conn.  sent TTFB    DL
/api/user         h2     200      0    142     118  1    61      4
/api/orders       h2     200      0    0       0    0    4       2
/static/app.js    h2     200      0    0       0    0    310     0
/static/app.css   h2     200      0    0       0    0    0       88
```

**Read it:**
- `/api/user` shows `Initial connection 142 / SSL 118` — it was the **first** request on a new connection, so DNS was cached (`DNS 0`) but TCP + TLS were fresh.
- The next three requests show `0` for connect and SSL: they reused the connection and were multiplexed.
- **The critical finding:** `app.js` has `Waiting 310` and `app.css` was sent at t≈4. That is a **head-of-line / dependency ordering** problem, not a server problem — the JS was issued late because the HTML had to be parsed, or because the CSS was render-blocking and the JS was discovered after it. The 310 ms is the app's own waterfall, not the network's.
- `app.css` shows `Content DL 88` with no `Waiting` — it was queued behind a busy stream on the same connection and downloaded immediately once it got a slot. This is HTTP/2 multiplexing working: no extra connection, no extra handshake.
- **Fix the JS:** inline critical CSS, add `<link rel="preload" as="script">`, or move the fetch to a `103 Early Hints` response. The network is doing its job.

## Drill 6: `openssl s_client` with a version mismatch

```
$ openssl s_client -connect legacy.example.com:443 -servername legacy.example.com </dev/null
CONNECTED(00000003)
error:1408F10B:SSL routines:ssl3_get_record:wrong version number
```

**What happened:** the server sent something that wasn't a TLS record — almost certainly a plaintext HTTP response.
**What it implies:** three possibilities, in order: (1) you used the wrong scheme — the endpoint is HTTP on 443 (or the port is a plain-HTTP port); (2) the server is doing plain HTTP and expecting `http://` on a nonstandard port; (3) you hit a different service entirely (an LB health endpoint, a misrouted port). **Diagnose:** `curl -v http://legacy.example.com:443/` and `nc -v legacy.example.com 443` to see the first bytes. `wrong version number` is a transport-level mismatch, not a certificate or cipher problem.

## Drill 7: `openssl s_client` with an incomplete chain

```
$ openssl s_client -connect shop.example.com:443 -servername shop.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^(depth|verify|Verify|New,|Server Temp|subject=|issuer=)'
depth=1 O = Example Root CA, CN = Example Root CA
depth=0 CN = shop.example.com, O = Example Ltd
verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate
subject=CN = shop.example.com, O = Example Ltd
issuer=CN = Example Issuing CA, O = Example Ltd
Server Temp Key: X25519, 253 bits
New, TLSv1.3, Cipher is TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
```

**What happened:** the leaf is present and forward secrecy is on (`Server Temp Key: X25519`), but the chain is one link short — the **intermediate is missing** (`depth=0` leaf, then jumps to the root which isn't a locally trusted issuer either).
**What it implies:** the server sent only its leaf certificate. Browsers often work anyway (they cache intermediates, or fetch them via the certificate's AIA extension), which is why this is a "works in Chrome, fails in curl" bug. **Fix:** configure the server to send `fullchain.pem` (leaf + intermediate), never just the leaf. The `Server Temp Key` line confirms you're on an ECDHE key exchange with forward secrecy.

## Drill 8: A Wireshark-style summary

```
No.     Time        Source          Destination     Protocol  Info
1       0.000       10.0.0.5        203.0.113.1     TCP       SYN  [Seq=0] [Win=64240]
2       0.0584      203.0.113.1     10.0.0.5        TCP       SYN,ACK [Seq=0] [Ack=1] [Win=65160]
3       0.1168      10.0.0.5        203.0.113.1     TCP       ACK [Ack=1] [Win=64240]
4       0.1168      10.0.0.5        203.0.113.1     TLSv1.3   Client Hello (SNI=api.example.com, ALPN=h2)
5       0.2337      203.0.113.1     10.0.0.5        TLSv1.3   Server Hello, Certificate, CertVerify, Finished
6       0.2921      10.0.0.5        203.0.113.1     TLSv1.3   Finished
7       0.2921      10.0.0.5        203.0.113.1     HTTP2     HEADERS  :method GET, :path /v1/orders
8       0.4089      203.0.113.1     10.0.0.5        TCP       1448 bytes
9       0.4090      203.0.113.1     10.0.0.5        TCP       1448 bytes (retransmission)
10      0.4674      10.0.0.5        203.0.113.1     TCP       1448 bytes  ← out of order delivery
11      0.7602      203.0.113.1     10.0.0.5        TLSv1.3   [Application Data]
```

**Read it:**
- RTT is ~58 ms (packets 1→2, 4→5). Confirmed.
- Packet 6 (client Finished) at 0.2921 arrives **after** packet 5 (0.2337) + 58 ms — so the client sent Finished in the *next* flight. That means this was a **1-RTT** handshake, not 0-RTT (in 0-RTT the client's application data would ride in the same flight as ClientHello, and you'd see it before packet 5).
- Packet 8 is a **retransmission** of the same 1448 bytes one microsecond later — that's a duplicate, indicating either a mirror port, a retransmit timer, or a capture on both ends. Combined with packet 10 arriving before the retransmitted data, the sequence is consistent with **one lost segment**.
- **The consequence is the point of the drill:** the response (packet 11) is delayed to 0.7602 — roughly 350 ms after the request — almost entirely because TCP had to recover the loss. This is **TCP head-of-line blocking**, and it's exactly what HTTP/2 cannot fix and HTTP/3 eliminates. A lost packet on an HTTP/2 connection delays *unrelated* streams.
- Packet 8 at 1448 bytes also hints at **MSS/MTU**: 1448 + 52 bytes of headers = 1500. If your path MTU were 1400, that segment would be dropped and never recovered cleanly.

## Drill 9: `ss -tan` state dump

```
$ ss -tan | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
  41230 ESTAB
   8841 TIME-WAIT
   1204 CLOSE-WAIT
    311 SYN-RECV
     47 LISTEN
```

**Read it:**
- `CLOSE-WAIT: 1204` is the **alarming** number. `CLOSE_WAIT` means the peer sent FIN and your application has not called `close()`. That is a **file descriptor leak in your code**, not a network problem. 1204 of them will become 1204 leaked sockets and, if the app isn't recycling workers, eventual `EMFILE`.
- `TIME-WAIT: 8841` is high but is on the *client* side here (connections we initiated), and it's mostly a symptom of not reusing connections.
- `SYN-RECV: 311` means 311 half-open connections are queued — either normal during a handshake burst, or a **SYN flood / accept backlog exhaustion** if it persists.
- **Fixes:** for `CLOSE_WAIT`, find the handler that forgets to `close()` (or use a framework with proper lifecycle); for `TIME_WAIT`, enable keep-alive/connection pooling and `net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1`; for `SYN-RECV`, check `net.core.somaxconn` and the listen backlog, and consider `tcp_syncookies`.
- **Verify the `CLOSE_WAIT` diagnosis:** `ss -tanp state close-wait` shows the owning process, and `lsof -p <pid> | grep TCP` shows the leak.

## Drill 10: Server access log timing fields

```
203.0.113.10 - - [01/Oct/2026:09:14:02 +0000] "POST /api/checkout HTTP/2.0" 200 812 "-" "curl/8.5.0"
  rt=1.842 uct=0.002 uht=0.011 urt=1.838 cs=MISS rid=01JB2Q7W3K9F
203.0.113.10 - - [01/Oct/2026:09:14:02 +0000] "GET /api/user HTTP/2.0" 200 1024 "-" "curl/8.5.0"
  rt=0.012 uct=- uht=- urt=0.010 cs=MISS rid=01JB2Q7WA2M4
203.0.113.10 - - [01/Oct/2026:09:14:03 +0000] "GET /healthz HTTP/1.1" 503 0 "-" "kube-probe/1.29"
  rt=0.001 uct=- uht=- urt=- cs=- rid=01JB2Q7WB7C1
```

**Read it:**
- Line 1: `rt=1.842`, `urt=1.838` — the app took **1.838 s**. `uct=0.002` means connecting to upstream was 2 ms, so the app was up. This is a slow application or database, not a network or connection problem.
- Line 2: `uct=-`, `uht=-` with `urt=0.010` — upstream was reached but the header-time field is `-`. That combination usually means the upstream sent headers in a way nginx couldn't timestamp separately (a very fast response). `rt=0.012` vs `urt=0.010` means only 2 ms of proxy overhead — good.
- Line 3: `urt=-` and `rt=0.001` — **the request never reached upstream**. A `503` from nginx with `-` in `urt` is a load balancer with **no healthy upstreams**, or a `limit_req` rejection, or the request was rejected by `server_tokens`/size checks. `/healthz` returning 503 to a `kube-probe` means the readiness probe is failing and the pod is about to be removed from rotation.
- **Implication:** the `kube-probe` 503 is a *consequence*, not a cause. The cause is upstream. Correlate by timestamp and by `rid`.

## Drill 11: A header set with a CORS mismatch

```
$ curl -i -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/orders \
    -H 'Origin: https://app.example.com/' \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...'
HTTP/2 200
access-control-allow-origin: https://app.example.com
content-type: application/json
vary: accept-encoding

{"id":"ord_9f3"}
```
Browser console:
```
Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/v1/orders' from origin
'https://app.example.com/' has been blocked by CORS policy: The
'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header has a value
'https://app.example.com/' that is not equal to the supplied origin.
```

**What happened:** the `Origin` header the browser sent was `https://app.example.com/` **with a trailing slash**, and the server's allowlist contains `https://app.example.com` without one. Origins never have a trailing slash — and the browser derives `Origin` from the *page's* origin, which is serialised without a path, so a page loaded from `https://app.example.com/` still sends `Origin: https://app.example.com`. The **curl** request is the one that added the slash, which is why curl "worked" and the browser didn't: the real mismatch here is that my allowlist has no trailing-slash variants, and the trailing slash in the curl command made me think it matched.
**What it implies:** allowlist entries must be exact serialised origins — scheme + host + optional port, **no trailing slash, no path**. Compare with strict string equality, never prefix or suffix matching. And the fix that prevents recurrence: normalise the allowlist at startup (parse each entry and compare scheme/host/port), plus a test that asserts the exact `Origin` values your app is allowed.
**Note also:** `vary: accept-encoding` but **no `vary: origin`**. If a CDN caches this response and serves it to a different origin, the browser will reject it — that's a second, intermittent CORS failure you'd have chased for days.

## Drill 12: `nc` and a raw HTTP/1.0 request

```
$ printf 'GET /healthz HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n' | nc api.example.com 80
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx
Content-Type: text/plain
Connection: close
ok
```

**What happened:** an HTTP/1.0 request (no `Host` header) to a modern server. nginx responded `HTTP/1.1` and added `Connection: close`.
**What it implies:**
- The absence of `Host` should get a `400` from a strict HTTP/1.1 server. nginx served it anyway, which is a deliberate compatibility choice. **Implication:** a request without `Host` can hit the **default server block**, which is often not the one you want. If you have a catch-all `server` block with a permissive policy, it's now reachable by IP with no host validation.
- `Connection: close` proves the connection is **not** being reused: HTTP/1.0 defaults to non-persistent unless the client sends `Connection: keep-alive`. Every such request pays a full TCP handshake.
- **Practical:** any HTTP/1.0-only client (old health checkers, some libraries) gets no keep-alive and doubles your connection count. Either require HTTP/1.1 at the edge or accept the cost knowingly.
- `Server: nginx` leaked: `server_tokens off;` would suppress the version. Minor, but it's free.

## Drill 13: A TLS 1.2 client hitting a TLS 1.3-only server

```
$ openssl s_client -connect new.example.com:443 -tls1_2 </dev/null
CONNECTED(00000003)
no protocols available
```

**What happened:** the client only offered TLS 1.2; the server's `ssl_protocols TLSv1.3;` config means no overlap.
**What it implies:** this is a **server-side policy** failure, not a client bug, and it's exactly what a strict-minimum policy does. Diagnose it in the browser by looking for `ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR` or `ERR_TLSV1_ALERT_PROTOCOL_VERSION`. **Trade-off:** `TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3` costs you nothing in modern clients and keeps old ones working; `TLSv1.3` alone is more secure but breaks anything older than ~2019, including some embedded devices, old Android WebViews, and a surprising number of enterprise scanners and monitoring agents. The senior answer is: enable 1.3, keep 1.2 with only AEAD ECDHE suites, and monitor what actually still negotiates 1.2 before dropping it.

## Drill 14: `Alt-Svc` and a browser pinning HTTP/3

```
$ curl -sI https://big-cdn.example.net/index.html | grep -i alt-svc
alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=2592000
```

**What happened:** the origin advertised HTTP/3 availability for 30 days.
**What it implies:**
- On the next visit, the browser will attempt QUIC to UDP/443. If it succeeds, it **pins** HTTP/3 for that origin for 2592000 seconds, and won't try QUIC again even if it later fails.
- If the QUIC attempt **fails**, the browser falls back to TCP and, critically, **does not retry QUIC for the rest of the `ma` window** in some implementations. So a transient UDP block can cost you 30 days of HTTP/3 for that user.
- **Implication for rollouts:** start with a short `ma` (e.g. 300), verify your handshake success rate, then extend. Never advertise `h3` unless a real QUIC listener exists.
- Confirm what the client actually did: DevTools Protocol column (`h3`) or a `chrome://net-export` capture.

## Drill 15: Reading a `504` from the edge against a healthy origin

```
edge access log:
  rt=30.011 uct=0.001 uht=- urt=- status=504
origin log (same rid):
  no request received
origin health: 100% CPU, 4 workers, event loop lag 2400ms
```

**What happened:** the edge waited 30 s (`proxy_read_timeout 30s`) and gave up; the origin never logged the request.
**What it implies:** this is a **starvation** signature, not a network one. The origin is at 100% CPU with 2.4 s of event-loop lag, so the request either never got scheduled or was queued behind synchronous work. `uct=0.001` says the connection to upstream was fine. **The distinction that matters:** a 502 would mean the connection failed; a 504 with no origin log entry means the origin accepted the connection but never got round to the work. **Fix:** find the blocking code (`perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay`, `--cpu-prof`), move it off the event loop, and scale workers. Then alert on origin-side "no log entry for an edge 504" as a distinct signal from a real upstream failure.

## Drill 16: A REST resource with a cache header bug

```
$ curl -sI https://api.example.com/v1/reports/2026-09
HTTP/2 200
cache-control: private, max-age=300
vary: accept-encoding
content-type: application/json

$ curl -sI https://api.example.com/v1/reports/2026-09 -H 'Authorization: Bearer user-a'
HTTP/2 200
cache-control: private, max-age=300
```

**What happened:** an authenticated, per-user response is marked `private, max-age=300`.
**What it implies:**
- `private` is **correct** — it forbids shared caches (CDN, corporate proxy) from storing it. Good.
- But `max-age=300` still lets **the user's own browser** cache it for 5 minutes. So if the user logs out and someone else uses the same machine within 5 minutes, the report is served from the HTTP cache. For a per-user financial or health-adjacent response, that is a data-leak-adjacent bug.
- The missing `Vary: Authorization` doesn't matter *here* because `private` already excludes shared caches — but it becomes critical the moment someone changes this to `public`.
- **Correct pattern for authenticated per-user data:** `Cache-Control: private, no-store` (or `no-cache` if you want conditional revalidation with an ETag). If you want a short cache, use `private, max-age=60, must-revalidate` and accept the risk consciously.
- **Also missing:** `Vary: Origin` if the response is CORS-relevant, and any `ETag`. Add `ETag` + `Cache-Control: private, no-cache` if you want the best of both: revalidate every time, but only transfer on change.

## Drill 17: A DNS delegation with no glue

```
$ dig +trace example.com 2>&1 | tail -20
example.com.		172800	IN	NS	ns1.provider.com.
example.com.		172800	IN	NS	ns2.provider.com.
;; received authoritative response for example.com
;; BADCOOKIE: no cookies received
example.com.		3600	IN	A	203.0.113.10
```
And separately, `dig @a.gtld-servers.net example.com NS +noall +answer` returns NS records but `dig NS ns1.provider.com` returns SERVFAIL, while the same lookup against the provider's own resolver succeeds.

**What it happened:** the NS targets are **out of bailiwick** (they're in `provider.com`, not `example.com`), so no glue is required — the parent has no A records for them. This is legal, but it means resolution depends entirely on the TLD server's cache.
**What it implies:** a resolution delay or failure happens if `provider.com`'s own nameservers are slow or if the TLD's cache of the out-of-bailiwick NS is cold. The fix is **in-bailiwick nameservers with glue**: delegate to `ns1.example.com` and put A records for `ns1.example.com` in the parent zone. **Rule of thumb:** always use in-bailiwick nameservers. The "out-of-bailiwick to avoid needing glue" advice is a common and expensive mistake.
**Also note:** the `BADCOOKIE` line is harmless — a recursive resolver's DNSSEC cookies weren't echoed because the authoritative server doesn't use cookies. Don't chase it.

## Drill 18: A gRPC call over HTTP/2 read from a packet trace

```
HEADERS  :method POST  :path /shop.v1.OrderService/GetOrder  :authority orders.internal:50051
          content-type application/grpc+proto
          te trailers
          grpc-timeout 250m
          authorization Bearer eyJhbGci...
          user-agent grpc-node-js/1.9.0
          <DATA frame: 00 00 00 00 0f 0a 0b 4f 72 64 65 72 5f 31 32 33 3e 3e 3e 00>

HEADERS  :status 200  content-type application/grpc+proto
          grpc-encoding identity
          <DATA frame: 00 00 00 00 2c ...>

HEADERS (trailers, END_STREAM)
          grpc-status 5
          grpc-message Order not found
          grpc-status-details-bin CiQKD...
```

**What happened:** a well-formed gRPC unary call that **failed with `grpc-status: 5` (NOT_FOUND)** while the HTTP status was `200`.
**What it implies:**
- The first `00 00 00 00 0f` is the **length-prefixed message framing**: 1 byte compression flag (`0`) plus a 4-byte big-endian length (`0x0f` = 15 bytes). Without this, Protobuf couldn't be parsed from a stream.
- The request `DATA` frame arrives **after** the `HEADERS` in the same flight because gRPC can't know the message length before it has the headers. This is the `te: trailers` requirement made visible: without `te: trailers`, a conforming server must reject with HTTP 400, because status has nowhere else to go.
- **`HTTP 200` with a failed call is the whole lesson.** Any HTTP-level monitoring, any load-balancer health check, and any retry middleware keyed on status code will treat this as success. Only `grpc-status` carries the outcome.
- The client sent `grpc-timeout: 250m` (250 ms). If the server had exceeded it, you'd see `grpc-status: 4` (DEADLINE_EXCEEDED) and a `RetryInfo` in `grpc-status-details-bin` — and the server should have cancelled its work.
- `grpc-status-details-bin` is base64. Decoding it gives a `google.rpc.Status` with machine-readable `ErrorInfo` — far more useful for a client than the human-readable `grpc-message`.
